explain.say: Do you know the word namaste? It is a friendly hello used in India and Nepal. Look at the board: na, ma, ste. In the Devanagari script, used for Hindi, Marathi, Nepali and Sanskrit, each of those chunks is one block. Writing goes in syllables, not single letters!

explain.say: Here is the big idea. Look at the first box on the board: क, said ka. Every consonant comes with a built-in a sound. You don't write the a, it is already there! A script like this is called an abugida. What do you think happens if you want ki instead?

explain.say: Look at the second box: कि, ki. A little vowel sign, called a matra, is added to the letter, and it changes the a to i. Different signs make ku, ke, ko. It is like giving the letter a hat or a tail. Can you see the curl?

explain.say: Now look at the third box: the top line. Most Devanagari letters hang from a line across the top, called the shirorekha, like washing on a line. When letters join into a word, the line joins too. Have you seen Hindi writing on a sign or a film poster?

faq.a: An abugida is a script where each consonant carries a built-in vowel, usually a, and other vowels are shown with small signs added to it. Devanagari is an abugida.
A matra is a vowel sign added to a Devanagari consonant to change its vowel, so क ka becomes कि ki or कु ku.
Hindi is written in Devanagari, from left to right. Consonants carry a built-in a, vowel signs change it, and most letters hang from a line across the top.

faq.q: Why do Hindi letters hang from a line?
faq.a: The top line, called the shirorekha, is part of most Devanagari letters. When you write a word, the lines join into one long bar, so the word looks connected.
Hindi, Marathi, Nepali and Sanskrit are among the languages written in Devanagari, used by hundreds of millions of people.

facts: Devanagari is used to write Hindi, Marathi, Nepali and Sanskrit, and is read from left to right.
Scripts with built-in vowels, called abugidas, include Devanagari, Tamil, Thai and the Ge'ez script of Amharic.
